Celestial navigation, visualized
Sight Reduction Sphere
A primer on finding your position from the sky, and a single-file 3D app that puts every step on screen.
A globe, a calculator and a chart in one page
3D globe
Three.js Earth inside a celestial sphere, with the PZX triangle and circles of equal altitude drawn live.
Sight-reduction panel
Hc, Zn, GHA, declination and LHA recomputed every second from the current UTC time.
Plotting sheet
The intercept method on a ±2° local sheet: AS, intercept and one LOP per observed body.
One index.html, opened directly in a browser. Three.js, fonts and Earth imagery come from CDNs; Sun, Moon and planet textures are embedded and render offline.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Overview
Latitude is local. Longitude is time.
Latitude needs one angle and no clock: the altitude of the celestial pole equals your latitude.
Polaris, or the Sun at local noon corrected for declination, has given latitude since antiquity: astrolabe, cross-staff, quadrant, sextant.
Longitude is the difference between your local time and the time at a reference meridian.
Without an accurate reference clock there is nothing local to measure. Ships ran on dead reckoning, with errors growing every day at sea.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
Four seconds of clock error, one mile of position
1ʰ
→ 15° of longitude
1ᵐ
→ 15′ of longitude
4ˢ
→ 1′ of longitude
Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, and at the equator 1′ of longitude is about 1 nautical mile. A clock drifting a few seconds a day puts a ship many miles off after a multi-week Atlantic crossing.
Nautical mile: exactly 1,852 m by international definition (1929). It began as one minute of arc of latitude along a meridian, so 1′ of latitude is always about 1 NM, while 1′ of longitude shrinks with cos(latitude).
1 NM ≈ 20 000 km / 180° / 60′ = 20 000 km / 10 800 ≈ 1 852 m

The quest for longitude
Year
Event
1707
Scilly naval disaster: roughly 1,400–2,000 lives lost to a longitude error
1714
British Longitude Act creates the Board of Longitude and its prize
1750s
Tobias Mayer's lunar tables make the lunar-distance method practical
1761
Harrison's H4 sea trial to Jamaica keeps time to seconds over weeks
1767
First Nautical Almanac, with lunar-distance tables (Maskelyne)
1773
Parliament awards Harrison £8,750; the Board never grants the full prize
1884
International Meridian Conference fixes Greenwich as 0°
Two rival answers ran side by side well into the 19th century: the lunar-distance method (no new hardware, long calculation) and the marine chronometer.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
The Moon as a clock
The Moon moves about 0.5° per hour against the stars: fast enough to notice, slow enough to measure precisely with a sextant.
01
Measure the angle from the Moon to the Sun or a star
02
Look it up in the Almanac's lunar-distance tables
03
The table gives GMT at that instant
04
Compare with local time from the Sun's altitude
05
The time difference is your longitude
GMT is the missing ingredient for longitude. Every calculation asks what the sky looked like from Greenwich at the instant of the sight.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
Sky coordinates: GHA and declination
Declination is the sky's latitude: angle north or south of the celestial equator.
Greenwich Hour Angle is the sky's longitude, with a twist.
GHA is always measured westward from the Greenwich meridian, and because Earth keeps turning it grows continuously with time.
The app recomputes GHA and Dec for the Sun, Moon and planets from the current UTC time.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
Stars: Aries and SHA
Stars are effectively fixed, so each gets a constant catalog coordinate.
SHA is measured westward from the First Point of Aries (the vernal equinox). SHA and Dec barely change for a given star; GHA of Aries carries all the time dependence.
GHA★ = GHA♈ + SHA★  (mod 360°)
The app stores J2000 RA and Dec and precesses them to the date of observation.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
Observed altitude and two horizons
Hs is the sextant angle from the visible horizon up to the body.
Zenith distance = 90° − Hs
The sensible horizon is tangent at the observer; the celestial horizon is parallel to it through Earth's centre. For such distant bodies the two point the same way.
Dip from height of eye is corrected separately; it is not part of the spherical triangle.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
The noon sight: wait for the peak
At Local Apparent Noon the Sun crosses the meridian and its altitude peaks.
Track the sextant altitude and wait for it to stop rising. No longitude and no accurate clock needed.
That is why latitude by noon sight was routine long before longitude was solved.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
Why the noon sight gives latitude
Sun rays at the observer and at Earth's centre are parallel, so Dec is the same angle at both.
Lat = (90° − Ho) ± Dec
Same name (Dec and latitude on the same side of the equator, Sun between zenith and equator): add Dec.
Contrary name: subtract Dec.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
Local Hour Angle: move to your meridian
The triangle is solved at the observer's meridian, not Greenwich's.
LHA = GHA + λE LHA = GHA − λW  (mod 360°)
LHA, declination and assumed latitude are the three inputs to sight reduction.

Pub. 229 and Pub. 249 tabulate Hc, a rate factor d and azimuth angle Z for every whole degree of latitude, LHA and declination.
Hc = Hc(tab) + d × Dec′ / 60
Compare Hc with Ho for the intercept; convert Z to true azimuth Zn by hemisphere rules. The app's sightReduce() does this in closed form, with no rounding or interpolation.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  Primer
The instrument
The Sextant
A hand-held angle-measuring tool that sights a celestial body against the horizon, giving the observed altitude (Hs) this app corrects and reduces.
What the application shows
Earth
NASA Blue Marble photo, ocean specular mask and normal map over an offline-safe procedural map.
Day and night
A live terminator from the computed Sun position, with city lights on the night side.
Bodies
Photo textures for the Sun, Moon and planets; stars in catalog colours, all labelled.
Sky frame
Celestial sphere, equatorial and ecliptic planes, poles, Greenwich meridian, starfield.
PZX triangle
Pole, zenith and the body's GP, with Hc, Zn, GHA, Dec and LHA alongside.
Circles and LOPs
Circles of equal altitude on the globe; one coloured LOP per observed body on the sheet.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  The application
One file, four layers
1
Markup and styling
Header toggles, left input sidebar, centre 3D viewport, right plotting sheet and values; a kiosk mode.
2
Astronomy math
Julian date, Sun and Moon models, star catalog, planet elements, GHA/LHA/GP, sight reduction.
3
2D and 3D geometry
Canvas plotting sheet, lat/lon to Cartesian, great-circle slerp, markers, arcs and planes.
4
Lifecycle and events
rebuildScene() recomputes and redraws; a one-second timer keeps UTC and every value live.
Camera moves update only the camera; astronomy is recomputed only when inputs or time change.

Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  The application
The sight-reduction formulae
L assumed latitude · D declination · H local hour angle
sin Hc = sin L sin D + cos L cos D cos H
cos Z = (sin D − sin L sin Hc) / (cos L cos Hc)
Zn = 360° − Z  if sin LHA > 0,  else Z

Side
Meaning
Value
PZ
colatitude
90° − sL
PX
polar distance
90° − sD

zenith distance
90° − Hc
s = +1 for the North pole, −1 for South.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  The application
The plotting sheet and the intercept
One minute of altitude is one nautical mile, so the altitude difference is a distance.
a = (Hs − Hc) × 60 NM
Positive: plot toward the body's azimuth. Negative: away. The line of position runs through the intercept point at Zn + 90°.
Δlat = d/60 · cos b Δlon = d · sin b / (60 cos lat)
A square ±2° around the DR position, north up, AS joined to DR by a dashed line. A local flat approximation: right for this window, not a map projection.
Every visible body with an Hs entered gets its own coloured LOP, independent of the focus body's.
Sight Reduction Sphere  ·  The application
Educational, not certified
  • Approximate Sun, Moon and planet ephemerides
  • No parallax for the Moon or planets
  • No refraction, dip, index error, semi-diameter or height of eye
  • No nutation, aberration, light-time or proper motion
  • Compact, approximate star catalog
  • Illustrative imagery, not navigational charts
For real navigation
Compare results with an approved nautical almanac and apply the complete sight-correction workflow.
